title: Use 80/20 as a Prioritization Hypothesis
subtitle: Look for concentration, then verify it.
description: Rank the few inputs most likely to matter, test that ranking against observed results, and revise it instead of treating 80/20 as a law or exact forecast.

lifeOsSource.hack: Treat 80/20 as a prompt to look for concentration, not as a promise that exactly 20 parts of input create exactly 80 parts of output.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Define one outcome, list the inputs that could influence it, rank a small number by expected impact and cost, choose one to check, and compare the observed result with your initial ranking. Revise the ranking when the data disagrees.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Which input actually changed the outcome, what did it cost, and what should move up, down, or out of the priority list?

faq.question: Does the result need to match 80/20 exactly?
faq.answer: No. The ratio is a memorable heuristic for uneven contribution. Your real distribution may be different; inspect it rather than force it to match the label.
faq.answerHtml: No. The ratio is a memorable heuristic for uneven contribution. Your real distribution may be different; inspect it rather than force it to match the label.

intro.html: The 80/20 idea is most useful as a question: is a small part of this system carrying a disproportionate share of the result? It is not a universal ratio. Use it to create a ranking you can challenge with real observations.

sections.title: 1. Name the outcome
sections.html: Choose one observable result and avoid optimizing a proxy unless you can explain why it matters.

sections.title: 2. Rank plausible inputs
sections.html: List the activities, customers, causes, features, channels, or failure modes that could drive the outcome. Rank a small number by expected impact, cost, and confidence. Mark guesses as guesses.

sections.title: 3. Check one priority, then re-rank
sections.html: Choose a reversible action that checks an important item near the top. Decide what you will observe first, compare what happened with the ranking, and update the list.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace an inherited Pareto article containing pseudo-precise effect sizes, arbitrary work intervals, fabricated observations, and ROI-style claims with a bounded prioritization exercise.
